metadata.title: Why Does the Moon Create Two Ocean Bulges, Not One?
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: The Moon pulls the oceans toward it. Why is there also a bulge on the far side of Earth?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, so the water on the side facing the Moon bulges toward it. That much seems natural. But look at the far side of Earth.
beats.new_visual_element: Earth (deep blue with teal land) with a thin translucent water layer; a grey cratered Moon on the Earth-Moon line; an ink arrow from the near-side water toward the Moon labeled 'Moon's gravity'; the near-side water bulges toward the Moon.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: Earth, Moon, near bulge, gravity arrow

beats.narration_text: There is a second bulge on the far side, pointing directly away from the Moon. If the Moon's gravity only pulls toward the Moon, why does water pile up on the side facing away from it?
beats.new_visual_element: The far-side water bulges outward, away from the Moon; a crimson question mark beside it.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: Earth with two bulges, Moon, gravity arrow, question mark

beats.narration_text: Gravity weakens with distance. Compare the Moon's pull at three points along the line to the Moon, drawn greatly exaggerated: the near side, Earth's center, and the far side. The near side is closest, so it is pulled hardest. The center is pulled less, and the far side least of all.
beats.new_visual_element: Earth fades to an outline with its diameter along the Earth-Moon line. Three arrows toward the Moon: long (ink) at the near point, medium (slate) at the center, short (ink) at the far point.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: Earth outline, diameter, three pull arrows of decreasing length

beats.narration_text: Earth as a whole falls toward the Moon with the acceleration of its center, so subtract the center's pull from each point. On the near side, what remains points toward the Moon. On the far side, what remains points away from it. Relative to Earth's center, both sides are pulled outward.
beats.new_visual_element: The diagram splits into two panels (stacked in 16:9, side by side in 9:16): near pull vs center pull with a teal difference arrow pointing toward the Moon; far pull vs center pull with a teal difference arrow pointing away. The two teal arrows then move back onto Earth's near and far points.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: Earth outline with teal tidal arrows at near (toward Moon) and far (away) points

beats.narration_text: That difference in pull, the tidal force, stretches the oceans along the line to the Moon and raises two bulges at once. As Earth turns beneath them, each coast passes through both. Two bulges, one cause: gravity that pulls unevenly.
beats.new_visual_element: Earth returns in full color with both bulges stretched along the teal tidal arrows; the land turns slowly beneath the fixed bulges; label 'tidal force = difference in pull'.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final: rotating Earth, two fixed bulges, tidal arrows, Moon, label
